p1.title: Passage 1
paras: The intensifying frequency and volatility of extreme weather events serve as the most visceral manifestation of anthropogenically driven climate change, breaking free from the abstract metrics of global temperature averages. Meteorological anomalies—ranging from stagnant atmospheric high-pressure systems that lock in catastrophic heatwaves to hyper-intensified marine deluges—are no longer statistically isolated deviations but systemic recalibrations of the earth's biosphere. This new climate paradigm exposes the deep fragility of global infrastructure, which was fundamentally engineered under the flawed assumption of environmental stationarity. Urban centers, coastal defenses, and agricultural heartlands are routinely overwhelmed by ecological forces that collapse legacy protective barriers. The economic cascading effects are equally destabilizing, as systemic crop failures trigger food insecurity while escalating property destruction threatens the solvency of global insurance markets. Humanity is caught in a high-stakes race against feedback loops, where melting permafrost and retreating ice caps reduce global albedo, locking in further thermal absorption. Mitigating this existential crisis demands a fundamental shift from reactive disaster response to deep, systemic climate resilience and decarbonization.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: Fitness has come to be associated with special places and special clothing: the gymnasium with its machines, the running track, the class that meets at six in the morning. These have their uses, but they can obscure a simpler truth. For most of human history people were active not because they exercised but because their lives required it. They walked to fields and markets, carried water, ground grain and climbed hills. Physical activity was woven into the day rather than added to it as a separate task.

Many people today spend their waking hours seated, at a desk, in a vehicle or before a screen, and then try to compensate with an hour of vigorous effort. The hour is worth having, but it may not undo the effects of the remaining sedentary day. A growing body of opinion holds that the small movements of daily life matter more than was once assumed: climbing stairs instead of taking the lift, walking to the shop, standing up every half hour, doing household chores by hand. Such activity is unglamorous and earns no medals, but it has the advantage of being sustainable, since it demands no fees, no equipment and no special motivation. The aim, perhaps, is not to become an athlete but to recover a little of the ordinary movement that modern convenience has quietly taken away.

questions.q: The author uses the phrase "environmental stationarity" to describe:
opts: The belief that climate patterns stay stable and predictable over time.
Weather systems stuck over one region.
questions.why: Vocabulary in context: infrastructure was built on the 'flawed assumption' that the climate would not change. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: What is the direct consequence of the reduction of "global albedo" mentioned in the passage?
opts: More heat absorbed by the earth, adding to warming.
questions.why: Detail: 'locking in further thermal absorption'. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

Proof that old climate models worked.

questions.q: The passage suggests that the best approach to modern climate risk is:

Decarbonization together with proactive, systemic resilience.

questions.q: Which title best suits the passage?
opts: Why Exercise Is a Waste of Time
questions.why: Main idea: ordinary daily movement, once 'woven into the day', deserves to be recovered.

opts: They were advised to by physicians.

questions.q: The author suggests that an hour of vigorous exercise after a seated day:
opts: Fully cancels the effects of sitting.
Is useless and should be avoided.
Is more sustainable than daily movement.
Is worth having but may not be enough by itself.

questions.q: The phrase "modern convenience has quietly taken away" suggests that:
opts: Convenience has made people more active.
The loss of everyday movement happened gradually and largely unnoticed.
People deliberately chose to stop moving.
questions.why: Inference/tone: 'quietly' implies the change crept in without people noticing.
Vocabulary: people 'spend their waking hours seated, at a desk, in a vehicle or before a screen'.
